label: Socket
description: Turn this program into a WebSocket endpoint. A caller opening a socket at the path starts a fresh execution: the opening request comes out on the fixed ports, and every message the caller sends is one item of the `inbound` stream, so a Loop over it runs once per message. Answer with Reply per message and Close at the end, or hold the conversation through the ctx in a custom node. One connection is one run; two callers never share a run.

inputs.name: path
inputs.label: Path
inputs.description: The route under the project's live URL: literal segments and `{name}` captures (`chat/{room}`). Required, and never empty: a trigger with no address would answer at the project's own address, where every other one that forgot would answer too. Must not start with '/'.

inputs.name: dataType
inputs.label: Message shape
inputs.description: What each message is, both ways: `json` (declare `inbound: Generator[JsonDict]`; declare `Generator[Image]` and a message that is a `data:` URL or base64 is stored on the way in), `text` (a String per message, `Generator[String]`), or `bytes` (each binary frame stored as a file, its stored-file value per message, `Generator[File]`).

inputs.name: auth
inputs.description: Who may open a socket here: wire an auth access node (ApiKeyAuth, JwtAuth, HmacAuth). Unwired, the socket is open to anyone with the URL. The gateway checks the opening request before a run starts and the established identity comes out on `caller`.

inputs.name: outlivesCaller
inputs.label: May outlive the caller
inputs.description: Who owns the run, which decides what a caller leaving means. Off (default): the run is the caller's, so their leaving cancels it, and a node that hits a long durable wait holds the worker briefly and is then killed rather than parked. On: the run is its own, so the caller leaving does not touch it and a long wait parks properly and resumes later, making it a background job. Be deliberate about it: the caller leaving is what ends a tied run, so switching this on removes that ending and whatever the run is still doing must end by itself. Work that finishes on its own is fine; anything that watches, subscribes or loops until something changes is not, and then you say what ends it, with `maxSessionSecs` here or a TagRun and StopTagged pair in the graph.

inputs.name: defaultHoldSecs
inputs.label: Hold seconds before giving up on a wait
inputs.description: For a caller-tied run: how long a node's wait holds the worker (keeping the connection alive) before giving up. Per-wait overrides win over this. Never unbounded.

inputs.name: maxSessionSecs
inputs.label: Give up on one connection after this long
inputs.description: A ceiling on one whole connection, off by default and with no default on purpose: it ends a connection on the clock whatever the caller is doing, so it would cut a live session short. A socket carries the protocol's own ping, which the other side answers, so a caller who leaves is found without this. Leave it alone unless you want a hard limit on how long one session may last.

inputs.name: callerSilenceSecs
inputs.label: Call the caller gone after this much silence
inputs.description: How long the caller's machine may leave what the worker sent it unacknowledged before the connection is called dead, in seconds. This is NOT a ceiling on the session: a machine that is still there acknowledges every packet by itself, whatever the person is doing, so a caller who stays resets this constantly and a socket held open for hours is never touched. It bounds SILENCE, which is the only way to tell a caller who vanished (a closed laptop, a dropped network) from one who is simply quiet. Raise it for a client on a link that genuinely goes silent for longer, like a device that sleeps its radio between messages; lower it to notice a departure sooner. `0` leaves the machine's own default, which is about fifteen minutes.

inputs.name: journalEphemeral
inputs.label: Keep the conversation out of the journal
inputs.description: What the journal keeps of what was said. Off (default): every message both ways is recorded, so the inspector replays the conversation. Messages are gathered a second at a time rather than written down one by one, anything over 100 KB is recorded trimmed, and raw bytes are never recorded whatever this says. On: only the sizes and the counts are kept, never the content. Turn it on for a socket carrying something you would rather not have written down, or one whose traffic is high enough that the sizes tell you what you need; remember you are also giving up seeing what was said when you debug.

outputs.name: path
outputs.description: The path as called under the project (no leading slash).

outputs.name: params
outputs.description: The `{name}` captures of the route's path, by name.

outputs.name: query
outputs.description: The opening request's query parameters, by name.

outputs.name: headers
outputs.description: The opening request's headers, by lowercase name.

outputs.name: caller
outputs.description: Who the auth gate established: a JWT's claims, `{"key": <index>}` for an API key, `{}` for an HMAC. Null when the socket has no `auth`.

outputs.name: inbound
outputs.description: One item per message the caller sends, in order; the stream ends when the caller disconnects. Declare the item type to match `dataType` (`-> (inbound: Generator[JsonDict])`, `Generator[String]`, `Generator[File]`). Wire it into a Loop's `over` to run the body once per message. A second reader of the same socket uses the ctx in a custom node (inbound is broadcast there).

then.message: Socket '{id}' path starts with '/'. The gateway prefixes the route automatically; drop the leading slash.

Socket '{id}' starts a run that never answers its caller: no Reply, Stream or Close is in it. Wire the answering node so the run reaches it (through data, or `_should_flow` on the node or on the group it sits in); a custom node answering through the ctx is the one case to ignore this.
